rationale: Perm is a tiny, recursion-heavy arithmetic benchmark from the Stanford suite with no source metadata available, so the table favors cheap, universally applicable transformations and discounts passes whose benefit depends on structure the profile cannot confirm. SUB is weighted highest since instruction substitution is nearly free, applies to any arithmetic code (which a permutation enumerator is full of), and carries minimal size/runtime/correctness cost. FLA and BCF get strong security/diversity weights because recursive permutation logic is control-flow dense, making flattening and bogus-control-flow highly disruptive to static analysis; their runtime weights are kept moderate because Perm's hot recursion must stay acceptable. SPLIT is cheap and low-risk, so it is kept as a low-cost diversifier even though its security contribution is modest. IBR and ICALL add indirection-based resistance with acceptable overhead on small functions. IGV is effectively disabled (low security/diversity weights, elevated costs) because the empty profile gives no evidence of global-variable usage to protect, so its runtime and size costs would be paid for little gain, and its higher correctness risk is not worth taking on an unverified codebase.
